plan.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) vs dulaglutide (Trulicity) in the SURPASS-CVOT randomized heart-outcomes trial (NEJM 2025): adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, about 13,300 people, median follow-up about 4 years. Covers the main heart and stroke result, death from any cause, A1C and weight, stomach side effects and stopping rates, what a non-inferiority trial with an active comparator can and can't tell you, and questions to ask your prescriber or cardiologist.
plan.angle: Keep the planned structure, with these changes. Working title: 'Mounjaro vs Trulicity for Heart Disease: What the SURPASS-CVOT Trial Found'. Thumbnail stays 'FEWER HEART EVENTS?' with subtext 'tirzepatide vs dulaglutide · type 2 diabetes'. Opening: 'about thirteen thousand adults with type 2 diabetes and heart or blood-vessel disease', the exact per-arm primary rates, HR 0.92 and CI from the NEJM paper, then 'not worse than dulaglutide; it did not prove it was better.' Second payoff: death from any cause per arm, said to be a secondary outcome that can't confirm a benefit on its own. plan.working_title: Mounjaro vs Trulicity: Which Protected the Heart More?
plan.why: An approved-drug head-to-head against tirzepatide (our best long format), with real brand-name search demand, built on one settled NEJM randomized trial that is easy to fact-check first time. It doesn't overlap with the dropped Serious Risks video, today's hair, gallbladder and diarrhea Shorts, or any live video. | fact-check: The trial is real and the topic fits the channel, with good evidence behind it. SURPASS-CVOT was published in NEJM on 17 Dec 2025 (PubMed 41903177). It was a double-blind, active-comparator, non-inferiority trial in adults with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, median follow-up about 4 years. The primary outcome was cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke. Rates were about 12% on tirzepatide and 13% on dulaglutide, HR 0.92: non-inferior (p=0.003) but not superior (p=0.09). Death from any cause was lower on tirzepatide, a secondary outcome. A1C fell 1.66 vs 0.88 points and weight fell 11.6% vs 4.8%. Tirzepatide had more GI adverse events, and overall adverse events were similar. Fixes needed before scripting: (1) Population size. 6,586 + 6,579 = 13,165 were randomized, so 'about 13,300' is wrong. Use 'about thirteen thousand' or the paper's exact randomized count. (2) The title 'Which Protected the Heart More?' suggests one drug won. The trial did not show superiority, so use a neutral question that doesn't hint at a winner. (3) Death from any cause must be framed as a secondary outcome that does not prove benefit. Use the paper's exact hedge and CI, and don't call it 'lower risk of dying' without that hedge. Never put it in the title or thumbnail. (4) Take the exact per-arm rates, HR and 95% CI from the NEJM paper, not from news coverage. (5) Name Eli Lilly (maker of both drugs) as the funder. (6) Section 1 of each label: Trulicity's US label carries a cardiovascular risk-reduction indication (from REWIND). Check whether the live Mounjaro PI (27 Aug 2026) has added a CV indication, quote only what it prints, and never imply an indication from this trial. (7) The trial arm labels (tirzepatide up to 15 mg vs dulaglutide 1.5 mg) are the dose limit; no other dose talk. (8) The 'Don't switch' safety line is good. Keep the no-switching framing all through: the video compares trial results, not which medicine to choose. (9) Confirm no existing SURPASS-CVOT or Trulicity long video is on the channel.

script.working_title: Mounjaro vs Trulicity for Heart Disease in Type 2 Diabetes: What the SURPASS-CVOT Trial Found
script.hook_pattern: Counterintuitive claim, answer first. Sentence 1 names Mounjaro vs Trulicity and gives the hedged verdict ("not worse, but not proven better"). The per-arm primary rates come by about 16 s. Death from any cause (8.6% vs 10.2%, framed as a secondary outcome over about 4 years) comes by about 30 s. One open loop (why "not worse" than this rival is a tough test) pays off in the toughest-rival chapter.

visual.stock_query: older man confused by two newspapers

scenes.retention_device: Relatable thread introduced, with a mini-loop

scenes.narration: So what does not worse actually mean? It is the phrase headlines trip over.
SURPASS-CVOT was a non-inferiority trial. Its main question was not which drug is better, but whether tirzepatide was no worse than dulaglutide, within a margin set in advance.

visual.stock_query: line drawn on track, finish zone

scenes.narration: Think of a relay team tryout. A challenger does not have to beat the team's best runner; it only has to prove it is not meaningfully slower.

visual.stock_query: relay tryout, two runners side by side

scenes.narration: Tirzepatide passed that test. The paper reports a p-value of zero point zero zero three for non-inferiority.

visual.stat_label: Non-inferiority test, tirzepatide vs dulaglutide: passed

scenes.narration: Then came the harder question: was it actually better? That test came back with a p-value of zero point zero nine, which did not reach the bar for proving it.

visual.stat_label: Superiority test, tirzepatide vs dulaglutide: not met

scenes.narration: A hazard ratio below one leans toward tirzepatide, and exactly one would mean no difference. The range here ran from zero point eight three up to one point zero one, so it still included no difference.

visual.stock_query: number line with range crossing one

scenes.narration: In absolute terms, the gap was less than one percentage point: twelve point two versus thirteen point one percent. That could be a real difference or chance, and this trial could not settle which.

visual.stat_label: Gap in heart events, tirzepatide vs dulaglutide

scenes.narration: So the honest summary is not 'Mounjaro wins' and not 'Mounjaro loses.' Mounjaro held its own.

visual.myth: Mounjaro beat Trulicity on heart events

scenes.retention_device: Myth correction pays off Ray's headlines

scenes.narration: One detail matters for trust: the trial was funded by Eli Lilly, which makes both tirzepatide and dulaglutide. It was also double-blind, so neither patients nor their doctors knew who got which drug.
The trial also has edges. It studied adults with type two diabetes and established heart or blood-vessel disease, so it does not directly answer questions about people without diabetes.
And because there was no placebo group, it cannot tell you directly how tirzepatide compares with no treatment at all for heart risk. Hold onto that gap; it matters later.
scenes.retention_device: Plants a callback for the rival chapter

scenes.narration: Labels matter too. Section one of the Mounjaro label lists a use to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type two diabetes who are at high risk for these events.

visual.quote: to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular (CV) events (CV death, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), or non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus who are at high risk for these events.

scenes.narration: Only the FDA-approved label says what a medicine is approved for, so ask your prescriber whether either label's uses fit you.
But that confidence range was not the only number to watch. The number people love to share comes next.
Back to death from any cause, because it is the number that gets stretched.

Death from any cause was eight point six percent on tirzepatide versus ten point two percent on dulaglutide: a hazard ratio of zero point eight four, with a confidence range from zero point seven five to zero point nine four.

visual.stat_label: Death, any cause, tirzepatide vs dulaglutide; CI 0.75 to 0.94

scenes.narration: That whole range sits below one. So why can it not count as proof? Here is where it gets interesting.

Death from any cause was a secondary outcome, and it was not adjusted for testing many outcomes at once. On top of that, the main test for being better was not met. So this number can point somewhere, but it cannot prove a benefit on its own.
Think of it as a second clue in a mystery: worth noticing, worth following up, but not enough to close the case.
So a headline saying Mounjaro proved it saves more lives than Trulicity goes further than this trial can.

visual.myth: Mounjaro proved it saves more lives
visual.fact: Secondary outcome; can't confirm a benefit alone

scenes.narration: For Ray, that is actually useful. It gives him a sharp question for his cardiologist, instead of a headline to panic or celebrate over.
But the numbers where the two drugs pulled far apart were blood sugar and weight.
Start with A1C, the blood test for longer-term blood sugar control.
After thirty-six months, A1C had fallen by one point six six points on tirzepatide versus zero point eight eight points on dulaglutide.
scenes.on_screen_text: A1C at 36 months: tirzepatide vs dulaglutide

visual.stat_label: A1C change at 36 months (points): tirzepatide vs dulaglutide

scenes.narration: Dulaglutide's drop was a solid step. By our own arithmetic, tirzepatide's drop was nearly twice that size.
Weight moved too. By thirty-six months, body weight had fallen by eleven point six percent on tirzepatide versus four point eight percent on dulaglutide.
scenes.on_screen_text: Weight at 36 months: tirzepatide vs dulaglutide

visual.stat_label: Body weight change at 36 months: tirzepatide vs dulaglutide

scenes.narration: For someone weighing two hundred pounds, that works out to roughly twenty-three pounds versus about ten. That is our illustration, not a result from the paper.
scenes.on_screen_text: Our math, 200 lb person: ~23 vs ~10 lb

scenes.narration: If you have spent years feeling judged about your weight, those numbers might feel like relief. Just remember that weight is one health measure among many.
scenes.retention_device: Name the feeling, then validate it

scenes.narration: So tirzepatide moved A1C and weight further. Why did that not show up as a clearly bigger heart benefit? This trial cannot tell you why; it stays an open question.
And there was a trade-off, one you might already feel in your stomach.
Every medicine has a cost, and here the cost showed up in the gut.
Gastrointestinal adverse events, the stomach and gut group, were reported by forty-two point five percent on tirzepatide versus thirty-five point nine percent on dulaglutide.

visual.stat_label: GI adverse events: tirzepatide vs dulaglutide

scenes.narration: At the same time, the paper reported the overall rate of adverse events as similar in the two groups.
And thirteen point two percent stopped tirzepatide because of adverse events, versus ten point one percent on dulaglutide.

visual.stat_label: Stopped for adverse events: tirzepatide vs dulaglutide

scenes.narration: If you have had that queasy week after a dose step, sitting at dinner and pushing your plate away, this will not surprise you. You are not imagining it.

visual.stock_query: woman pushing plate away at dinner

scenes.narration: Your prescriber can help with practical ways to make stomach symptoms easier, so bring them up instead of quietly putting up with them.
Which brings us back to the promise from the start: why is being not worse than Trulicity a bigger deal than it sounds?
scenes.retention_device: Reopens the main loop before the payoff

scenes.narration: Because Trulicity is not just any rival. It had already passed its own heart trial.
In the REWIND trial, adults aged fifty or older with type two diabetes and either cardiovascular disease or cardiovascular risk factors got dulaglutide or a placebo shot.

scenes.narration: Heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death happened to twelve percent on dulaglutide versus thirteen point four percent on placebo, over a median of about five years, a hazard ratio of zero point eight eight.

scenes.narration: That result backs the heart use on the Trulicity label. Section one lists a use to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type two diabetes who have established cardiovascular disease or multiple cardiovascular risk factors.

visual.quote: to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, or non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus who have established cardiovascular disease or multiple cardiovascular risk factors.

scenes.retention_device: Exact label wording, the last new fact

scenes.narration: So tirzepatide was not racing a dummy shot. It was racing a runner who already had a medal, and it kept pace.

So where does that leave Ray? Whichever of the two shots he takes, it has been tested in people with type two diabetes and heart risk like his, and the choice between them belongs in a conversation with his care team.

Here is the whole trial in three lines.
In adults with type two diabetes and heart or blood-vessel disease, tirzepatide was not worse than dulaglutide for heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death, and it did not prove it was better.
It lowered A1C and weight more than dulaglutide did, and gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent on tirzepatide.

scenes.narration: Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber. And please, do not switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.
These are prescription medicines, so talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether one is right for you.

If you came here worried that your weekly shot is the wrong one, here is the calmer truth: both drugs were studied hard in people with type two diabetes and heart risk, and your next step is a good conversation, not a panic.

factcheck.summary: I checked the script's numbers against the trial paper and the drug labels, and they hold up. The SURPASS-CVOT figures (NEJM 2025;393:2409-2420, PMID 41406444) match: 13,299 adults randomized; 12.2% vs 13.1% for heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death; HR 0.92 (95.3% CI 0.83–1.01); P=0.003 for non-inferiority and P=0.09 for superiority. So do the median of about 4 years, double-blind design and Lilly funding. Death from any cause was 8.6% vs 10.2% (HR 0.84, 0.75–0.94), a secondary outcome not adjusted for multiplicity. At 36 months, A1C fell 1.66 vs 0.88 points and weight 11.6% vs 4.8%. GI adverse events were 42.5% vs 35.9%, overall adverse events were similar, and 13.2% vs 10.1% stopped because of adverse events. REWIND (12.0% vs 13.4%, HR 0.88, median 5.4 years, age 50+) and both labels' Section 1 heart-risk wording also match: Mounjaro revised 8/2026, Trulicity revised 3/2026. Our own arithmetic (nearly twice the A1C drop; about 23 vs about 10 lb for a 200 lb person) is right and labelled as ours. Framing, safety lines and the Ray scenario (clearly hypothetical) are fine. One major issue: s9 says "not worse" than an active rival is a "tougher test" than beating placebo. That's wrong as a general statement, and the script itself says in s21 that it can't tell us how tirzepatide compares with no treatment. Three minor fixes follow.

issues.claim: being not worse than this particular rival is a tougher test than beating a dummy shot
issues.problem: Statistically, a non-inferiority result against an active comparator is a weaker claim than beating placebo, not a stronger one. The trial passed against a pre-set margin and had no placebo group, which s21 itself says. Calling it a 'tougher test' overstates the evidence and contradicts s21. The payoff in s52–s53 ('kept pace with a medal winner', 'real information, not a win') can stay because it is correctly hedged.
issues.fix: s9 narration: "And later, I will show you why being not worse than this particular rival means more than it sounds." s9 on-screen text: "Why this rival matters". s47 already matches this wording ('a bigger deal than it sounds'), so leave it as is.

issues.claim: Tirzepatide: not worse, not proven better
issues.problem: The opening card doesn't name the comparator or the outcome, so muted viewers can't tell what tirzepatide was compared with.
issues.fix: s1 on_screen_text: "Tirzepatide vs dulaglutide, heart events: not worse, not proven better"

issues.claim: Only the FDA-approved label says what a medicine is approved for, so ask your prescriber...
issues.problem: This is our own agency and safety line, not a label finding. Our own lines get no source tag.

issues.claim: There is a video I would watch next, linked in the description.
issues.problem: No watch-next target is named in the post notes. The publisher needs one that matches the drug and population.
issues.fix: Keep the s67 narration. Add to the post notes: "Watch-next target: Mounjaro vs Ozempic (SURPASS-2) long video (adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin)."
